## Overview

Backpressure is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

Without backpressure, fast producers can overwhelm slow consumers, leading to:
- Unbounded memory growth as items queue up
- Process crashes due to resource exhaustion
- Loss of data if buffers overflow

## Common Implementations

Backpressure can be implemented through several patterns:

### Bounded Queues
The producer writes items to a fixed-size queue. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer blocks until the consumer drains items, creating an automatic slowdown mechanism.

### Credit-Based Flow Control
The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items. The producer tracks its available "credits" and stops sending once credits are exhausted. The consumer replenishes credits as it processes items.

### Reactive-Pull Models
Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. This gives the consumer full control over the rate of consumption, eliminating the possibility of overwhelming a producer.

## Use Cases

Backpressure is essential in:
- Streaming data pipelines (e.g. Kafka consumers, message queues)
- Real-time processing systems
- Resource-constrained environments
- Systems handling bursty or uneven data sources
